problem: Pretrained VLN agents such as PREVALENT and VLN↻BERT learn object-level grounding well, but they learn action-level modality alignment only implicitly from instruction-path supervision. Action-level alignment means mapping a phrase like 'exit the bedroom' to the specific view that realizes the action (the bedroom door). Learning it only implicitly limits robust action decisions in new scenes.
motivation: Prompt engineering has given pretrained language and vision-language models new abilities simply by supplying suitable prompts. CLIP's zero-shot image-text alignment makes it possible to mine paired visual and textual 'action' evidence from training trajectories. The authors therefore give the agent explicit multimodal action prompts, so it can learn which views correspond to which instructed actions.
key_idea: Build a base of CLIP-mined (single-view image, action phrase) pairs from training trajectories, retrieve the ones relevant to each instruction, and encode them as extra tokens next to the instruction in VLN↻BERT. Two auxiliary losses align the image and text halves of each prompt and make the agent attend to the relevant prompt at each step.
insight: Adding prompts alone barely helps: in the R2R val-unseen ablation at 100K iterations, SR goes 60.4→60.5 with ResNet-152 and 61.5→61.6 with CLIP features. The auxiliary losses carry the gain. The InfoNCE modality-alignment loss lifts SR to 61.7 / 62.8, the sequential-consistency loss mainly raises SPL (to 56.1 / 56.6), and both together give 62.5 / 63.1 SR and 56.1 / 57.2 SPL. The appendix variants show where the value comes from: action-level prompts beat object-level prompts (Object: 59.9 / 61.9 SR); feeding prompts as extra training samples actually hurts (Extra: 59.0 / 60.7 SR); and taking image sub-prompts from Fine-grained-R2R sub-paths rather than whole paths reduces multi-object noise (Whole: 61.8 / 60.5 SR). Overall gains over VLN↻BERT are consistent but modest, about +1–2 SR/SPL.
method: Baseline agent: VLN↻BERT recurrent cross-modal transformer. A state token plus candidate-view features cross-attend to the instruction encoding X; self-attention scores over the candidates serve as the action probabilities. Visual features are ResNet-152 (Places365) or CLIP.

Action prompt definition: a modality-aligned pair made of an image sub-prompt (a single-view observation of a salient object or location on the ground-truth path, which implicitly encodes the action) and a text sub-prompt (an action phrase such as 'walk through the kitchen').

Prompt base construction: hand-built object/location and verb vocabularies are filtered from the R2R vocabulary. For each object word in a training instruction, CLIP zero-shot scores ('a photo of {CLASS}') pick the path view with maximum probability as the image sub-prompt. Nearest-verb search before the object word extracts the text sub-prompt. The base is built from Fine-grained R2R sub-instruction/sub-path pairs to cut multi-object noise, and is shared between R2R and RxR.

Prompt retrieval and encoding: action phrases are extracted from the test instruction and matched to base text sub-prompts by cosine similarity of CLIP text features, with retrieval precomputed. Up to N prompts are kept (max 60 for R2R, 100 for RxR, padded). Precomputed CLIP image and text features go through single-modal encoders E^i and E^u (linear + dropout), are concatenated, and pass through a multimodal encoder E^p. The resulting prompt tokens are concatenated to X to form X^p for cross-attention.

Modality alignment loss L_a: InfoNCE between the paired image and text sub-prompt features, with in-batch non-paired text sub-prompts as negatives. It is applied only during imitation-learning (IL) training.

Sequential consistency loss L_c: the cross-attention over X^p is split into instruction attention and prompt attention. An L2 loss pulls the attended text sub-prompt feature toward the attended instruction feature, and the attended image sub-prompt feature toward the attended visual feature, at each step. It is applied in both IL and reinforcement-learning (RL) training.

Training: L = L_RL + 0.2·L_IL + 0.01·L_c + 0.0001·L_a with AdamW and batch size 16. Training is two-stage: VLN↻BERT is first trained to convergence (lr 1e-5), then the best-SPL checkpoint is fine-tuned with ADAPT (lr 1e-6). Runs use 300K iterations for R2R and 100K for RxR.

setting.backbone: VLN↻BERT (PREVALENT-pretrained cross-modal transformer, fine-tuned) with ResNet-152 (Places365) or CLIP visual features; frozen CLIP used offline for prompt mining and sub-prompt feature extraction
setting.training_data: R2R train plus the same augmented data used by VLN↻BERT (PREVALENT augmentation) for R2R. English subset of RxR train (26,464 pairs) for RxR. The action prompt base is mined from Fine-grained R2R training sub-paths/sub-instructions with CLIP.
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views) with heading/elevation per view
setting.privileged: none (prompt base is built from training data only)

numbers_note: RxR is evaluated only on the English subset, with no RxR test results. RxR baselines marked * are the authors' re-implementation of VLN↻BERT. The R2R ablation table ('All models are trained for 100K iterations', e.g., ADAPT-Full val-unseen SR 62.5 / 63.1) and the low-data Scan/Instance table use shorter training and are not listed as separate entries. R2R SR/SPL are printed as integers.
results: On R2R, ADAPT (ResNet-152) reaches 64 SR / 58 SPL on val-unseen and 65 SR / 59 SPL on test-unseen, beating the strongest baseline VLN↻BERT (63/57 on both). On the English RxR val-unseen subset it improves the re-implemented VLN↻BERT from 45.5 SR / 39.3 SPL / 52.9 nDTW to 46.7 / 40.3 / 53.6. With CLIP features, ADAPT beats VLN↻BERT*(CLIP) on every metric (R2R val-unseen 66 vs 65 SR), though CLIP features lower test-unseen results for both models. In low-data settings (20–80% of scans or instances), ADAPT is generally 1–2 SR above the baseline.
limitations: The action prompt base is noisy: CLIP errors, scene complexity and instruction diversity yield imperfect image-phrase pairs (stated limitation).
Gains over VLN↻BERT are modest (about +1–2 SR/SPL). The method needs two-stage training from a converged baseline, hand-built vocabularies, and Fine-grained R2R sub-path annotations.
RxR evaluation is restricted to the English subset and validation splits; the method fails on ambiguous instructions such as 'walk forward and turn left' that name no landmarks.
